planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost; this vigorous, large-leaved selection is propagated vegetatively rather than from seed.

directions: Root 3-4 in semi-ripe cuttings in a sharply drained mix in late summer, or set out nursery plants in spring in lean, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Holt's Mammoth is a robust culinary sage selected for its unusually large, 4-5 in gray-green leaves and fast, vigorous growth, making it a favorite of growers who need to harvest big quantities of leaf for drying. Flavor is fully typical of garden sage — warm, resinous, and savory — and the plant produces attractive violet-blue flower spikes in early summer. Cut back hard in spring to remove winter-damaged wood and keep growth dense.

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery transplants after the last frost in lean, sharply drained soil; this cultivar is propagated vegetatively to preserve its pink flower color.

directions: Root semi-ripe stem cuttings in late summer, or plant container-grown starts in spring in full sun and lean, well-drained soil. Rosea sage is a low, bushy culinary sage selected for its pale lilac-pink flower spikes rather than the species' usual blue-purple, produced over a long season on typical wrinkled, aromatic gray-green leaves. Leaves are fully edible with the classic warm, savory flavor of common sage. Trim after flowering and again in spring to maintain a compact habit and prevent legginess.

planting.note: Grow on a moss pole or bark totem in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; the true species climbs steadily and holds a cool, matte silvery-blue-green leaf color even without the 'Silver Sword' cultivar selection.

directions: Grow on a moss pole or bark totem in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained, humus-rich aroid mix, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. Philodendron hastatum is a wild climbing species native to coastal rainforest in southeastern Brazil, distinguished by narrow, elongated, spear-shaped (hastate) leaves with a soft, matte, silvery-blue-green cast that darkens somewhat as leaves age. It is the true species behind the widely traded 'Silver Sword' selection, but unlike a single named cultivar it represents the full natural variation of the species as it occurs in habitat, climbing steadily up vertical supports on aerial roots and producing progressively larger leaves with height. Maintain moderate to high humidity and warm temperatures, and avoid exposure below 55F. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew) — Philodendron hastatum

common_name: Mexican Philodendron (Mexican Tree Aroid, Trilobed Philodendron)

planting.note: Grow on a moss pole or bark support in bright, indirect light in a loose, chunky aroid mix; Philodendron mexicanum climbs by adventitious roots and develops its most dramatic, deeply lobed leaves once it gains vertical height.

directions: Grow on a moss pole or rough bark support in bright, indirect light in a loose, chunky, well-drained aroid mix, watering once the top inch of media has dried. Philodendron mexicanum is a hemiepiphytic climbing species ranging from central and Gulf Mexico south through Guatemala, Honduras, Costa Rica, Panama, and into western Colombia, prized for its leathery, semi-glossy, arrow-shaped leaves with unequal, outward-flaring basal lobes that give each leaf a three-lobed silhouette, plus a distinctive maroon-tinted undersurface most visible on young growth. It climbs steadily with support, producing larger and more deeply lobed leaves as the plant matures, and tolerates a wide range of warm, humid indoor and greenhouse conditions. Feed lightly during the growing season and keep humidity moderate to high for best leaf form. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
sources: International Aroid Society — Philodendron mexicanum species profile
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Climbing philodendrons for shade

planting.note: Grow in bright, indirect light on a moss pole or trellis in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; unlike the self-heading 'Congo' cultivars bred from this species, true Philodendron tatei is a genuine climber and needs vertical support to look its best.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light on a moss pole or trellis in a chunky, well-drained, humus-rich aroid mix, allowing the top inch of media to dry between waterings. Philodendron tatei is a climbing species native to wet tropical forest in northern Brazil, Guyana, Peru, and Venezuela, with a thick stem, short internodes hidden by rusty (ferruginous) cataphylls, and glossy, leathery leaves borne continuously along the length of the climbing stem. It is the wild parent species behind the popular self-heading 'Congo' cultivar line — a subspecies selection that was bred to abandon climbing for a compact, rounded, non-vining habit — but the true species itself remains an actively climbing plant that should be given a support rather than grown as a clumping floor plant. Keep warm and humid, and protect from temperatures below 55F. CAUTION: toxic to cats and dogs.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew) — Philodendron tatei

common_name: Bonilla Big Bluestem (Northern Plains Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average soil in full sun; Bonilla was collected near Bonilla, South Dakota, and released cooperatively by NRCS, ARS, and the North Dakota, South Dakota, and Minnesota Agricultural Experiment Stations for its northern cold hardiness.

directions: Bonilla is a northern-adapted big bluestem release bred for reliable winter hardiness and strong forage and habitat quality across the Dakotas and Minnesota. It forms an upright clump of blue-green summer foliage topped by the turkeyfoot-shaped seed heads typical of the species, coloring bronze-red through fall and holding structure over winter. Because it establishes and overwinters more dependably than southern-source big bluestem in cold climates, it mixes well with cool-season prairie grasses in restoration and conservation plantings as well as naturalistic garden borders. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Pawnee Big Bluestem (Late-Season Southern Plains Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average, dry soil in full sun; Pawnee originated in Pawnee County, Nebraska, and is recommended for plantings from central Nebraska south through Oklahoma.

directions: Pawnee is a later-maturing big bluestem release valued for its deep green summer foliage, tall seed stalks, and strong forage production across the southern Great Plains. Growth peaks in midsummer heat and the plant reaches full maturity later in the season than most other named releases, giving it good heat and drought tolerance for hot-summer regions. It is a mainstay of Kansas and Nebraska prairie restoration seedings and works equally well as an upright, structural anchor plant in native and pollinator gardens. Cut the dormant clump back in late winter before new shoots emerge.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

common_name: Bison Big Bluestem (Early-Maturing Northern Plains Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained to average soil in full sun; Bison was selected in North Dakota for early maturity and reliable winter survival, and is best adapted to North Dakota and the northern halves of South Dakota and Minnesota.

directions: Bison is the earliest-maturing named big bluestem release, selected for uniform plant type, good leafiness, and strong vigor in short northern growing seasons. It tends to stay shorter at maturity than southern-source big bluestem or other northern releases like Bonilla, making it a more compact option for cold-climate prairie restorations and conservation seedings. Its early seed set and dependable cold hardiness suit it to North Dakota, Minnesota, and the northern Dakotas where longer-season selections may not reliably mature. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Forestburg Switchgrass (Northern Plains Upland Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Forestburg was collected near Forestburg in Sanborn County, South Dakota, and released in 1989 by NRCS, ARS, and the North Dakota, South Dakota, and Minnesota Agricultural Experiment Stations.

directions: Forestburg is a cold-hardy, upland-type switchgrass bred for reliable performance in the Dakotas, central and southern Minnesota, northern Iowa, and western Wisconsin. It forms a dense, upright clump of blue-green summer foliage on reddish-tinted stems, with airy, open seed panicles tinged pink to brown that mature to persistent tan plumes through winter. Its short rhizomes give it a tidy, slowly spreading habit useful for erosion control and wildlife cover as well as naturalistic garden plantings, and it tolerates both dry and seasonally wet sites once established. Cut the dormant clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Nebraska 28 originated in Holt County, Nebraska, and was released in 1949 by the Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station and the Soil Conservation Service.

directions: Nebraska 28 is an early-maturing, semi-decumbent switchgrass representative of the fine-stemmed strains native to the Nebraska Sandhills, bred for strong establishment on sandy, well-drained sites. Its earlier seed set and medium height make it well suited to shorter growing seasons across the Upper Midwest, and it has a long track record in pasture and conservation plantings for erosion control. The finer, more lax foliage provides valuable nesting and brood-rearing cover for ground-nesting birds along with bedding and travel cover for deer. Cut the dormant clump back in late winter before new shoots emerge.

common_name: Gone With The Wind Prairie Dropseed

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; like other prairie dropseed selections, Gone With The Wind is slow to establish and takes about three years to reach mature size, but is long-lived once rooted.

directions: Gone With The Wind is a Walters Gardens selection of prairie dropseed prized for its fine-textured, fountain-like mound of arching green leaves and abundant, wispy tan flower panicles that catch the slightest breeze. The late-summer blooms carry the same fragrance the species is known for, often compared to coriander or warm popcorn, and the foliage shifts to coppery red-orange tones as fall progresses. Its deep, drought-tolerant root system and dense clumping habit make it useful as a specimen, mass groundcover, or container planting, and mature clumps can persist for decades without needing division. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Joybera Series Gerbera Daisy (Extended-Bloom Proven Winners Patio Gerbera)

planting.note: Set out vegetatively propagated young plants after the last frost once nights have warmed, since Joybera is a Proven Winners series sold as started plants rather than grown from seed.

directions: Joybera arrives as a vigorous, vegetatively propagated Proven Winners selection, so gardeners set out young plants after the last frost rather than starting from seed. It produces an unusually high number of large, brightly colored daisy blooms in shades of red, orange, pink, and yellow that keep flowering longer and more continuously through the season than older florist-type gerbera. Grow it in full sun to part sun with excellent drainage, water at the base to keep the crown dry, and remove spent flower stems at their base to keep new buds coming. In colder regions treat it as a container or bedding annual, since it is reliably perennial only in zones 9 and warmer.

common_name: Cartwheel Series Gerbera Daisy (Fleuroselect-Awarded Semi-Double Seed Gerbera)

planting.note: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost at around 70F and transplant into full sun after hardening off, since Cartwheel is a true seed-propagated series rather than a vegetative clone.

directions: Cartwheel is a Fleuroselect-recognized seed series noted for its unusual semi-double, pinwheel-shaped flowers in pastel and bicolor shades rarely seen in ordinary gerbera seed mixes. Start seed indoors 8 to 10 weeks before the last frost at around 70 degrees F, barely covering the fine seed, and transplant into full sun and well-drained soil once nights have warmed. Its compact, uniform habit was bred for pot and bedding production, holding 3 to 4 inch blooms on sturdy stems over neat rosettes of foliage. Water from below to avoid crown rot, deadhead regularly, and treat it as an annual outside its hardy range or overwinter it indoors as a houseplant.

common_name: Princess Fabiana Alstroemeria (White Peruvian Lily Streaked with Burgundy and Cream-Edged Foliage)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots shallowly in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Princess Fabiana is a dwarf patio-bred selection from Konst Breeding's Princess Lily (Colorita) series.

directions: Princess Fabiana is a dwarf, patio-bred member of Konst Breeding's Princess Lily (Colorita) series, grown for its crisp white flowers streaked with burgundy and rose over the throat, set off by unusually decorative foliage edged in cream. Plant tuberous roots shallowly in spring in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, since like other Princess types it forms a shallower, more fibrous root system than full-size garden Alstroemeria. Pull rather than cut spent flowering stems from the base to trigger continuous reflowering through summer, and mulch the crown heavily over winter at the cold edge of its range or grow it as a container plant that can be moved under cover. Its compact, well-branched mound suits border edges and large pots as well as cutting for small posies.

common_name: Princess Eliane Alstroemeria (Compact Bright Pink Peruvian Lily with Maroon-Flecked Yellow Throat)

planting.note: Set tubers about eight inches deep in spring into fertile, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Princess Eliane is a compact selection from Konst Breeding's Princess Lily series.

directions: Princess Eliane is a compact selection from Konst Breeding's Princess Lily series, forming a low, mounding clump of lance-shaped foliage topped from early summer into autumn with clusters of bright pink, funnel-shaped flowers marked with maroon flecks over a yellow-orange throat. Set tubers about eight inches deep in spring into fertile, moist but well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, and avoid disturbing the shallow crown once established. Pull spent stems from the base rather than deadheading with shears to prompt further flushes of bloom, and mulch heavily for winter protection at the colder end of its hardiness range. Its naturally dwarf habit makes it well suited to patio containers and border fronts where larger Peruvian lilies would be too tall.
